title: Air India Losses More Than Double to Rs 22,238 Crore as Expansion Plan Meets Its Bill
excerpt: Air India and Air India Express lost Rs 22,238 crore in the year ended March 2026, up from Rs 10,859 crore a year earlier, even as new CEO Tewolde Gebremariam seeks more widebody aircraft and Tata Sons weighs a capital infusion of more than Rs 10,000 crore.
body:
• Air India and Air India Express posted a consolidated loss of Rs 22,238 crore in the financial year ended March 2026, more than double the Rs 10,859 crore loss a year earlier.
  • CEO Tewolde Gebremariam told an aviation summit in New Delhi on November 3 that the airline wants more widebody aircraft, while admitting its unit cost exceeds its unit revenue: "CASK for us is greater than RASK."
  • Tata Sons' board has approved in principle a fresh capital infusion of more than Rs 10,000 crore, subject to the airline presenting a business case, according to reporting cited by Urban Acres.
  • The pressure continued into the current year: the group's first-quarter FY27 loss exceeded Rs 6,000 crore, against more than Rs 3,000 crore a year earlier.

Air India's losses are testing whether the Tata Group and Singapore Airlines can finance a costly transformation while the carrier expands its fleet, refurbishes older aircraft and rebuilds its international network. Air India and Air India Express lost Rs 22,238 crore in the financial year ended March 2026, compared with Rs 10,859 crore a year earlier — an increase of about 105%.

The figures arrive as the airline pursues the expansion intended to fix it. Since the Tata Group took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022, the programme has included integrating the group airlines, refurbishing older aircraft, adding new planes and expanding international routes.

The New CEO's Diagnosis

Tewolde Gebremariam, the former Ethiopian Airlines chief who took over as Air India's CEO in August, outlined the twin priorities at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi on November 3: win back international passengers, and bring the cost of carrying them below the revenue they generate.

"CASK for us is greater than RASK. Need to improve RASK."

— Tewolde Gebremariam, CEO, Air India

CASK is the cost of providing a seat over a kilometre; RASK is the revenue earned for the same unit. Gebremariam's point is the airline's central problem in one line: flying each seat currently costs more than that seat earns. He said he expects profitability "very soon" and added, "I am more impatient than the shareholders about profitability."

More Aircraft, Longer Routes, Higher Costs

Even so, the expansion continues. Air India has commitments covering 80 widebody aircraft — 50 Airbus A350s, 20 Boeing 787s and 10 Boeing 777Xs — including about 10 delivered, and operates 61 such jets. Gebremariam confirmed discussions about further widebody purchases: "We want to increase our widebody order. Our network and strategy demand more widebodies." He did not disclose the number or types of additional aircraft, a timetable, or a date for profitability.

Network planning is being shaped by a cost the airline cannot control. Pakistan's airspace has been closed to Indian carriers since April 24, 2025, forcing longer routes to Europe and North America. Air India is considering concentrating Europe and North America services at Mumbai, growing toward Asia and Australia from Delhi, and developing Bengaluru as a third hub.

Who Pays

Singapore Airlines, which owns 25.1% of Air India, recorded a S$945.2 million share of Air India's losses in the year ended March 2026, according to its annual report. A Reuters report in August said Air India was seeking about $1.5 billion in fresh equity from Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines.

Tata Sons' board has approved in principle a fresh capital infusion of more than Rs 10,000 crore, according to an Economic Times report cited by Urban Acres, with the funding subject to conditions including the airline presenting a business case when it seeks the money. The airline has also been seeking around Rs 10,000 crore in fresh bank loans for fleet expansion, refurbishment and operating expenses. The final structure and timing of either proposal have not been established.

For passengers, the stakes are practical: the pace of refurbishment, the availability of new capacity and the strength of Air India's links between Indian cities and global hubs all depend on how the owners divide the financial risk. The first-quarter numbers — a loss above Rs 6,000 crore, against more than Rs 3,000 crore a year earlier — say the bill is still growing faster than the turnaround.
